As the Hormuz crisis waxed and waned, India walked a delicate tight rope in geo-strategy, while RBI did the hard lifting by selling dollars to prop up the Indian currency, which at one point veered dangerously close to the psychologically damaging 100 rupee (to one dollar) mark.

While RBI’s interventions, as well as the stabilisation of oil prices (it actually fell from a peak of $138 after the start of the war to $71 by July over the past couple of months) had made most of us believe that the worst was behind us, fresh clouds have blown in, very apparently in recent

As the world’s investors started chasing AI, foreign investment into the country has trickled out. And this couldn’t have come at a worse time — Trump tightening the screws on India on the trade front (including threats over buying Russian oil), the outgo of even more dollars to buy even less oil, and the subsequent drop in the value of the rupee which is like a domino effect going on to impact everything else.
Now top it with rural unease due to a bad monsoon, and all that it means in the coming months!

​Videos with alarming titles like "Urgently Leave India?" are designed around emotional urgency to drive engagement. Examining the specific claims in the video alongside broader economic realities helps separate clickbait from structural data:
​1. Inelastic Imports, Energy Deficits, and the Rupee
​The Video's Argument [01:03]: The creator points out that India runs persistent trade deficits because imports are inelastic—importing ~88% of crude oil, 50% of natural gas, significant fertilizers, and major defense hardware, putting continuous pressure on the rupee.
​The Context: India has been a net energy importer for decades. Despite elevated crude oil prices, India’s foreign exchange reserves stand near historic highs of ~$700 billion, providing roughly 11–12 months of import cover. Unlike past crises (such as 1991 or 2013), the Reserve Bank of India holds sufficient reserves to manage orderly currency depreciation without triggering a balance-of-payments crisis.
​2. Emerging Market Relative Performance & FPI Outflows
​The Video's Argument [01:54]: The creator argues that Indian equities lagged other emerging markets recently, noting that foreign investors pulled capital due to taxes (STT, LTCG, STCG [02:22]) and shifted funds abroad.
​The Context: Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) did engage in significant profit-taking and tactical rotation. However, this followed a multi-year period where Indian equities drastically outperformed most emerging market peers (especially China and Latin America). Global asset managers periodically rebalance allocations after periods of outperformance. Meanwhile, domestic systematic investment plans (SIPs) bring in over ₹25,000 Crore every month, providing a continuous domestic liquidity cushion that previous market cycles lacked.
​3. Capital Expenditure and Technology Investment
​The Video's Argument [02:06]: The video contrasts investments in AI (US) and semiconductors (Taiwan) with domestic issues in manufacturing and innovation.
​The Context: While the US and Taiwan lead in cutting-edge semiconductor fabrication and frontier AI models, India's capital expenditure cycle has focused heavily on physical and digital infrastructure: dedicated freight corridors, highway networks, power grid modernization, renewable energy installations, and domestic manufacturing under Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) frameworks. These investments are aimed at lowering domestic logistics costs and expanding industrial capacity over a multi-year horizon.
​4. Navigating Extreme Market Sentiment
​Online commentary tends to swing rapidly between extremes:
​During bull market peaks, commentary often turns euphoric ("Nifty 100k", "unstoppable super-cycle").
​During market consolidations or drawdowns, narratives frequently pivot to catastrophe ("collapse", "damage will take generations" [03:00]).
​Economic growth is rarely a straight line; it moves in cycles of expansion, digestion, and policy adjustment.
